requirement:
An item with no attachments has an empty list. A language may return empty
lists for every item.
rationale:
The requirement `requirements.sdk.outlines.attachments.empty` has two obligations. An item with no attachments has an empty list. A language may return empty lists for every item. The second is a MAY, so it imposes nothing to check.

The only reviewed test is `crates/trust-but-verify/tests/outline_content.rs#fn[bundled_languages_classify_only_their_attachment_syntax]`, which carries a `{test}` reference to the subject. It covers the first obligation in two ways:

- **Plain text:** The `test.txt` case has the source `# just text`, which looks like a comment but is not one in plain text. It expects no attachments at all, so every item's list must be empty.
- **Other languages:** In each language case, the test flattens the attachments of every outline item. It compares them to the exact expected `(kind, text)` list. Items that carry no expected attachment, such as the `const s` statements in the TypeScript cases and the rule `a { ... }` in the CSS case, therefore must contribute nothing. The test also asserts exact counts for specific items: `def[f]` has 3 attachments, and `class[C]` has its decorator as its first attachment. It never asserts per-item emptiness directly.

Under this setup, spurious attachments on items that should have none would break the equality assertions. The default is a `Vec` initialised empty. `OutlineItem::new` in `crates/trust-but-verify/src/outline/contents.rs` sets `attachments: Vec::new()`, and the field is a plain `Vec<OutlineAttachment>`. An item without attachments cannot be represented any other way. So the test is enough for this requirement. I found no gaps and no acknowledgments are needed.
